projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Flora Fieldman was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Today is May 19, 2007. I am the interviewer, an honored interviewer this morning. I'm really excited to be able to chat with you. Now, my name is Sandy Lacey; and Lacey is L-a-c-e-y for the reporter. And we'll be conducting these oral interviews, oral history interviews today, just one from you. And I will be here in Westminster, Colorado. I just moved here from Colorado -- excuse me, California. And you were talking about California earlier. I would like to introduce to the record Flora Fieldman. And she'll be spelling her name for our court reporter, who is Pat Boslough. I'm really honored to be here. I'm going to tell you at the beginning that I'm having a hard time because my dad was a World War II veteran on the front lines for three years. And he's on my mind because he's no longer with us. But he's gone ahead, and so I'll try to keep those emotions under control. It kind of makes it pretty nostalgic.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I would say so for myself too.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Did you have any chance to be interviewed before?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: No. Just all the stories here and by doing what is here.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Let me go ahead and start with Flora; and then I would like to tie everything together with Lisa, who would be Flora's daughter. And Pat, if I get going too fast, you know, I think, that you can slow me down. And then with Flora too. If I forget to ask you something that is important -- and Lisa too -- let me know so we get this right. Okay. So if you would state for our reporter your first and last name and spell your last name.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I'm Flora Fieldman, F-i-e-l-d-m-a-n. My maiden name was Hamilton; and most of the, you know, the tour of duty that I did was under my maiden name, Hamilton. But Fieldman is F-i-e-l-d-m-a-n.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: All right. And thank you for your extra information. And your current address?Flora Fieldman:: My current address is 5360 Newland Street, N-e-w-l-a-n-d, in Arvada, Colorado. ZIP Code is 80002.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay. And also, if you will, can you tell us your date of birth?

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: You were born the year of my dad. So we've got another thing in common. Before I can forget, I'd like to introduce Lisa --

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: Hamilton-Fieldman. I took my mother's maiden name.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman is Flora's daughter. Okay. We are honored to have you here.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Now, how many children do you have?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I have three daughters and one son.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay. So --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: The boy -- the boy was the youngest.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Three girls -- just kept trying until you got your boy?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I don't think that was the case, but I was not disappointed in the fact he was a boy.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Oh, no way. I'm sure not. I just -- before it gets away, we want to continue with the thank you that we started in the ceremonies this morning. Were you expecting all of this today?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: It was just an overwhelming experience. I was honored.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Was it?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yes, yes. I had no idea when I came out. I thought I would sit down, and I'd talk with you. And I'd tell my stories to the best of my memory and remembrance. And that would be it, you know, so I was really so -- I was really overwhelmed. It was nice to be acknowledged. I'm so ...

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I'm glad. It's such a condition of real importance that we do this. It's special. It's very special. I want to make sure I try to talk a little bit about the interest that we have here. But I do want to thank you personally for everything that you did for our country.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Can you tell us, just initially, about the civilian service. You were on a ship or --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: No. I was -- well, I'll start out where it began for me. We lived in the town of Roundup. My family was in Roundup, Montana, when Pearl Harbor occurred. And I remember I was ironing and just sort of -- everything just stopped that day. And, you know, so generally, my father was living in Missoula, Montana, at the time. And so we eventually followed him to Missoula. And I got there in the summer of '42 and took a part-time job, of course. I started my senior year of high school there.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: So, you are --

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: I think it was in the summer of '41. Because it was in December of '41 when Pearl Harbor happened.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Okay. My history's not too good.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: I think you had to be 18 at the time because you had turned 18 in November of '41.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. But I had been held back in school earlier, so I started that year of high school to finish and saw an ad in the Missoula newspaper about workers --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: -- defense workers. And I latched onto it and got in touch with the people that had the ad. It was for welders. And I signed up to go to this welding school -- for which I paid, of course -- and rode on my 19th birthday to Buckley, Washington, to enroll in the Buckley Welding School. And we were promised jobs when we finished our course, so I finished it. I learned to weld flat, vertical, horizontal, overhead, the works, and was certified by the time I went to Vancouver and began work in the shipyard. So that was the sequence; that's how I got into welder's school and then started in the shipyard. I started in the shipyard at the Kaiser Vancouver Shipyard in Washington; and it's across the river from Portland, Oregon. There is another, third shipyard in Portland that built only tankers. And then there was still another one. I'm not sure what that one did. When I was -- when I started in the shipyard, we had completed a PT boat contract; and we had finished building PT boats. And so next we tooled up then for aircraft carriers. They were not as big as the big aircraft carriers, these were what we called the "Jeep" aircraft carriers.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: They had a shorter flight deck, and they had a big launching mechanism to launch the planes and a restraining "Jeep" that attached to the tail of the plane as the tail landed. So the larger one had enough flight deck to, you know, accommodate an aircraft without that.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Looking at the photograph --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And you made 26 of these?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I have a few photographs, a number of the kind that we built.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That's overwhelming. How nice to be behind those guys and making everything safe for them.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. {Looking at photograph.} That was my badge, by the way.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That is where you have been a good historian.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: There it is, Mom. It's behind your hand.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: It is simply --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: -- beautiful.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: That is one of our ships. We launched them on the Columbia River.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I see. Wow. Thank you so much for sharing that. And I'm really appreciative, and I'm really grateful to you for taking these pictures.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Pictures of, you know, copies of pictures and things --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Anyway --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Can I ask a couple of little things; and then anything that you want to branch off into, I just want you to do that too.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Okay. I don't want to take you places that --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Well, I just really want to know what is important to you and what kind of particular events maybe stand out in your mind, stand out in your memory.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Okay. Okay.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: But I wanted to know where were you living at the time. I think you told me that. After Pearl Harbor, you know, before you actually left home.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Okay. I was living in Roundup, Montana, which is a small town in eastern Montana; but we were kind of in the process of moving to Missoula, which is in western Montana.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: You know, so we just kind of moved one by one -- my brother went -- my younger brother was first, my younger brother.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Did you not go to Missoula?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: My dad was there, and I went after my younger brother and then my sister. And my mom came later in the year --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: -- right before school started.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Did you already say your brother had joined the service?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: My younger brother joined the Navy, that is, after I had started the, you know, the job in the shipyards. And he joined the Navy --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Where did he do his boot camp?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: In the Great Lakes in -- out of Chicago, I think. And he eventually served on one of the ships we built.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That would be really special for you.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: He had not quite a Kamikaze hit, but a Kamikaze attempt.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Attempt?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: On his ship, right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Is this his ship, there? {Looking at photograph.}

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Wonderful. Why did you pick the service branch that you joined?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: You know --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Was that your only option?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: There was anything -- it was the ad in the paper and my feelings about doing something to, you know, to join the war effort.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: After Pearl Harbor, the Navy was really pretty crippled. And their ships were sunk and damaged, and so they needed ships in a hurry. And that's why we started building the smaller ships.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That makes sense, doesn't it?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And the PT boats -- not Liberty boats -- that's the kind that Jack Kennedy served on, but I didn't work on any of those. They were pretty much done by the time I started.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I see. Do you recall anything in particular about those first days -- how you felt, and just how everything was?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: No. Everything was kind of moving fast. We were assigned a crew, and what we did was we worked in crews which were, you know -- there were several women sections, and almost all of the welders in the section of the shipyard when I started -- which was the assembly building -- were women. I say it was a building -- it was a roof, it was open-ended and it was very, very long. And, you know, we were just assigned to a crew where we were needed -- whenever they needed an extra person because it was kind of -- you know, it was a process that was building as the people came on, you know, so it was as if every crew was, you know, complete as people came on.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Stable crews?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I see. And so your experience in the welding school, it was to function in this area?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. Right. If shipyards would have been training people to weld -- which I didn't know, of course, at the time -- I would have taken my course of study to get the training at the shipyard that I got in the welding school. And therefore, I didn't start as an apprentice. I started as a certified welder because I already knew the kind of welding that would be required of me.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: So you were one that others were looking up to?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Well, you know all of the welders, I think, most of them, probably had been through somewhat the same experience I had when I had gone to school. I didn't know -- we started as what they call tackers. We worked with a ship builder who -- when the material came in for the hull of the ship, this was flat. And then they had to gradually build, you know, the ribs, kind of.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: You had to build that, to shape it gradually into shape eventually with big hammers. And the welders, then, would make tacks on that to hold it in place until a production welder came along -- which I still was a production welder -- and fill the rest of the weld in. And then the finished section of the ship would be taken by cranes out to an open area where additional work might be done to it or it might be carried directly to the outfitters to be worked on or the ways where the actual ship dock was.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Is it waves or ways?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Ways.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay. Very good. So you had some more learning, some more training?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I didn't have more learning to do, you know. They used the welders for whatever particular task was necessary at the time in that particular -- we had -- we were in a bay -- it was a bay.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: bay was divided. It was about, oh, I think, 50, maybe 75 feet wide; and it was lined by banks of welding machines and, you know, gas. Some of that gas welding -- that was going on too. And all of the equipment, the power equipment was there that was being used in the bay. And the bay was over concrete. It was, like, railroad ties -- or not railroad ties -- railroad rails.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Maybe it was about three feet above concrete, and learning to walk across rails -- and if you didn't, you fell in -- you kind of -- nobody hurt themselves, but we all learned to do that. We wore boots. We wore heavy leather pants, leather jackets and, of course, we had the hoods. We all had our welding hoods.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: The welding hoods were for protection?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. Well, protection and for our hair.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That's very interesting.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: It went over the hair. We put our hair up in a scarf of some kind because you didn't want your hair to be out where it could be burned.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: You had protection for your eyes?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: dark lens was placed in the welding hood -- the hood over the dark lens. And you had to occasionally change your lenses because they would become pitted with little pieces of metal that eventually made it nigh impossible to see what you were doing. But all that, of course, was supplied.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And they probably checked on you frequently to make sure you were equipped properly.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: You know, I always had good lenses and what I needed.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And if there was a situation where you needed some medical attention?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: There was a clinic in the yard for burns or anything like that.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That's good. Okay. Let's see. What else do you want to talk about here? How did you feel when you arrived there and it all became real to you that you were going to be --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: The first night, it was kind of overwhelming. I came from a small town, and it was -- you know, finding housing -- they had built a lot of apartments for shipyard workers, and I roomed with another woman that was working there until I later found a room at a private home. And then, you know, that wasn't the only move. Immediately, it might have been strange, but there was so many other people that were in the same boat, figuratively, as far as experience and being away from home -- all of that. And I was homesick, I had to admit.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I'm sure you must have been.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And there were buses to take us to the shipyard, and then we had about a half a mile walk too, from the gate. And we had a pass -- this was our pass -- {Pointing to picture} -- that is how they knew that we belonged.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And a lovely photograph, by the way. We got to the photograph that I'd seen before. {Looking at photograph.}

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And so did you make some friends?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yes, we did. You know, we became friends with our --

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: Let me see your file. {Lisa assisting Flora locate pictures from paperwork.}

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: You're fine. Would the folder she's got help? We can go and find it.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Actually, there was a woman, a girl, a little older than I was, but in another crew that lived in and came from a city or from a town just outside of Missoula. Lola. So we became friends and, you know, as far as after hours, most of us were -- we were very tired and very dirty when we got finished; so there was not a whole lot of activity, especially not at first. As things went along, you know, there was more at this time; and you met more people. And I met guys and flirted and, you know, mostly just welders or shipfitters.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I'll bet that they were flirting too, judging by the photographs. And what was your friend's name?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Lola, L-o-l-a, Bottham, B-o-t-t-h-a-m.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That's great to know. Did you stay in touch after the war at all?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Well, we did for a patch; and I dated her brother for a while, you know.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: You, from time to time, went on a date? {Looking at photographs.}

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yeah. Preston Davis. I would have really gone for him; but he was into ships, boats. He was from a fishing family from up on the coast in Washington; and he was very, very much into fishing boats so -- but he worked there for quite a long time.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And being he was really into the boat thing --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: You know, I don't believe that was an issue. I think they are so single-minded that, you know --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Tunnel vision?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. And I had been up to his place on one of the weekends and up to where his family lived in Tokeland, Washington. And his sister and I had become acquainted. And his sister, who -- she was quite frail and not a well person; but she was a very sweet person. But at any rate, it didn't last.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: But it's a memory that you'll always have; isn't it? Now, where was that? Was that by --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: In Washington, Tokeland --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: How do you spell that?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: T-o-k-e-l-a-n-d. It's not by the city. It was a town on the coast.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: fishing village.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay. These are some beautiful pictures. Take a lot of time here.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Many of the people in the photographs there are no longer here.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Would you like to take a minute and have a drink of water? And we'll give the reporter a moment, and we'll get to take a look at your file now that it's here. {Brief break was taken.}

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: When I was a kid, we just went to country schools in eastern Montana. And we went to -- we had these Christmas plays in which the city schools got together too. Sometimes two schools would get together, and we were gathered at one of these plays, school plays. And somebody said to me, one of the adults said to me, You look like Katharine Hepburn. And I was just -- I thought, Oh, my goodness. Just wait until I tell my mom.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: What did your mom think?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Mom said, You have a better-looking mouth than Katharine Hepburn.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I was trying to figure out who it was you reminded me of.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Well, in the picture, I'm not exactly thin; and I'm a teenager. But at this time, I guess, I was on the thin side; and my cheekbones were high. And I was just so overwhelmed by this idea. But my mom was not. She was defending me, saying that she was the homeliest woman on the screen.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Oh, I don't think she was.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Well, I don't think so either; but my mom did.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That's important when your mom feels that way. Could you tell us about this picture? {Looking at photograph.} Tell us about your crew.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Okay. The front bunch is our crew, and this picture that was taken -- it was in the Bosn's Whistle, a little shipyard newspaper.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Bosn's what?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Just Whistle. B-o-s-n-'s Whistle.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That is really neat. Okay. You kept a really good record.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: At that time we were -- my crew was a "Hotshot" crew. We had gotten so good in welding that we got sent on any problem or special jobs and were transferred. And then we were in the "way" on what they call the "subways," that is, the area between the assembly -- where I had started out -- and the ways where the -- what do you call it? Anyway, the hull -- the structure that this ship was built in.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: Scaffolding?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. And we were sent to, you know, just whatever problem jobs needed particularly good welders. And then later on, we were transferred to the outfitters' deck which is the last stage that the ship is finally made ready for its trial run.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I see. And it looks like that is quite a procedure.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Well, the crew that I was on, my crew, was just a women's crew.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: The Hotshots?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: But the back crew {in photograph} was probably all made up of men because there were more men than not on the ways because of the climbing, the climbing and the heavy carrying into the ship. When I mentioned subways, that was the area between the bays in the assembly building where we worked most of the time and the area where some additional assembly was done out in the open before that section was picked up by cranes and transferred over to the ways. So there was an assembly building; and there was even another part that came before the assembly building where everything was marked and, you know, cut to shape before it came to us to put it into its final shape with ribs, or, you know, the -- some of this slipped my mind.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That's okay. You take your time. We can catch it later if it doesn't come back. I just want you to have a good time and relax. Those are wonderful photographs. I'm so grateful that they are in such good shape.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: These were the ships we built. {Looking at photograph.} We built -- we made 150 aircraft carriers.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: One, five, zero?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yes, 150. And my brother served on the 18th one that we built.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Did you get to see your brother at all?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Not at all until I got home. He was in the Navy, and I didn't get home very often. And toward the end of my stay in the shipyards, we worked ten hours a day, seven days a week. There was a real push. We worked ten hours every day.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Boy. Wow. I bet you had some complainers about that.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Oh, yes, there was. But really, people didn't complain. People did not complain.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Isn't that wonderful?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I knew and have seen some; but most of the crews, we hung together and put it out.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: It's fascinating.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: This was a C-4 there. {Looking at photograph.}

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: It was on its trial run in the photograph.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: How special is that.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Later christened to the United States fleet.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Here comes the lump again. Let me see.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Ships were very seldom launched on the swing shift, which is four to eleven.Sandra Lacey:: Four to eleven shift?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Anyway, it was called the swing shift; and we got off at 11:00 -- 10:30 or 11:00. And ships were not launched on the swing shift, but on the day shift. In other words, to get privileges to see one of your ships go down ways -- they cut it loose in the outlet. And it would be that we had to have a launch pass so that we could come in off of our own shift and get to see a launch.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Did you do that very often, Flora?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: No, just one of them.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: days' launching?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: It had to be days', every one of them was.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: What company did you say you were with?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Kaiser Company, Inc., Vancouver Yard, Permanent Bay.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I bet you did get off to go see one of the ships you built.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Now, this set of photographs -- tell me who was Frenchy?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Oh, he was a ship foreman; and he was kind of an overseer of the shipfitters. We were a crew of welders, and that was a crew of shipfitters. And we were told that he was the expert, of course; and he would see to it that the shipfitters were doing the right thing and got nothing over on him, you know.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay. Wonderful.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And he would always work in the derby.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: He used to wear the derby?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: He never was without that derby, ever.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Something to help you to remember him?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I'm not sure there was any hair under it. He always had the derby on his head.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And this is Mrs. Veberes. {Looking at photograph.}

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: How do you spell that?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: V-e-b-e-r-e-s. I lived with her in Vancouver for quite a while. She wanted someone to come in that was, you know, closer to her daughter's age. She had a daughter who was my age.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Mary?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And her daughter was mentally -- had mental problems, and Mrs. Veberes thought that having somebody her own age might be of some help. Mrs. Veberes had a son in the service. And he survived all those years of his service in Europe and died in a Jeep accident after the war was over.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Oh, my.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: It was really heart-breaking.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: So did you develop a close relationship?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: To some extent, but, you know, part of the problem was that I was gone a lot. I was, you know -- I was working and --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Most of your hours --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And so I did have to get some sleep.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: So you couldn't be there very much?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yeah, yeah -- I did get to be a very, very good welder. I got put on every -- I got put on jobs, you know, when somebody has goofed; and there is a lot of space to fill.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: You were the trouble shooter.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. And I got put in, you know, when we worked in the subways outside of the assembly building, there was these sections where you had to crawl down into a small space. You'd get a fan, you know, you'd have some kind of a floor; but I got most of these because I was small. And I had to, you know, get a lot of smoke.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Obviously you were not claustrophobic.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: No. No, I was not.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I can't imagine doing it if you were.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: We had to crawl between bulkheads, and it was a very small area. And I wasn't real tall, and they had small partitions in the -- we call them bulkheads. And you have to go and weld where you needed to. And you'd crawl through all of those bulkheads to get to where you were going. So it was tight; and I mean, it was not well ventilated. So I got a lot of smoke, which eventually led to me having to leave the shipyard.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Really? Can you tell us about that?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yes. Well, that was in '45. It was in the spring of 1945, and I had been, you know, coughing and wheezing and getting -- having various problems. And the people at the clinic, in the shipyard clinic, told me I really needed to quit getting in the smoke. And I thought well, if I'd have to quit doing what I was doing, I would have had to leave, you know, because they weren't terribly sensitive about, you know -- if you couldn't show up -- if you couldn't, you'd better not try to. There were no threats like that. It was simply the doctors in the clinic told me that I had to leave for my health.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: For your health? For your safety?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. And I was living with the Veberes family at the time.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay. So then where did you go at that point? What happened next?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I had bought a horse. We had frequent rallies in the shipyard, and people would sell various things. And this one was all about to raise money for the war savings bonds -- primarily war bonds they were called then. And somebody raffled off a horse. And the horse wasn't there, of course, but, you know, they could do that. They could sell a car that way with the object of encouraging people to buy war bonds. And the person who won the horse on the raffle, I got her name and bought the horse from her. And there was a little place -- I have a picture somewhere in my file.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I didn't see. The cabin?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. This was the cabin with a little car right out in front. {Per photograph.} Only two miles from the shipyard.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Perfect.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yeah. And I kept her there. I called her Red Lady.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Uh-huh. And look at you, standing so tall and proud of her, you were.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I rode her home to Montana.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: You didn't.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: 765 miles.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Oh, my goodness. I bet the war was not over, so there was no way you could ship anything that wasn't priority.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: You had to have a priority to transport anything, you know. The rationing of gas was still on, so transport was very limited to absolute necessity, you know.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And how old were you when you left?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I had to have been 20.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Twenty years old?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: But, you know, it was a safe trip because people were busy with the war. They were occupied, and so I didn't meet any problems on the road.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: What a blessing.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yeah. You know, if people think of doing something like that today, you're taking your life in your hands.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: So how long did it take you?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: 765 miles.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And it took how long?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I was gone -- was it three weeks?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: little over. I wasn't really keeping time. I had to leave for a couple of days to see a veterinarian because Red Lady had gotten bitten by what they call a Bots fly, B-o-t-s fly. And what they do is they leave an egg under the hide of the horse, and they call it a warble. And it became sore, so I had the warble removed and gave her a little time to heal up. And one place in my trip on the second -- I think it was the second day or maybe the third day out -- there's a great long hill, St. Mary's Grade. And it's not -- it's not that. It's Maryhill Grade. It was a Washington State Park -- it goes-- it has switch backs, and I had walked most of this because her back was still sore.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Pulling Red Lady along?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: She was more than willing, but at any rate, I didn't want to make her worse.Sandra Lacey:: What an interesting story. Did you ever have any experience at all during your trip that stands out in your mind? Did you ever have anything unusual happen?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: If there was no family, nobody I could stay with, I would just find a barn, you know, I'd just --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Rest and --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: For the most part, I tried to stay with families, you know.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I bet they were happy to have you and wanted to help you.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Oh, yeah, and curious. There's Maryhill Mountain the third day out on the ride home. {Looking at photographs.}

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: All by yourself.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Long road? {Looking at photographs.}

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And that's the Bridge of the Gods over the Columbia River. I didn't go across, but past it. You can see a little bit of my shadow.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Yes, I do see that. I'm glad you had a camera, Flora.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And a camera was one of the things that was rationed; you simply couldn't get them.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Is that where she ended up?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: That was where we ended up. Well, the last family I stayed with on my ride home from the shipyard was just outside -- was a few miles outside of the ranger station near St. Regis, Montana. They were by the ranger station, and the family suggested that I stop and, you know, ask about work for the summer, which I did. And that ended up my getting a job on the lookout, where that one is, for two seasons.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Wonderful.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Called Little Joe.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: There it is. It says the same on the photograph -- Little Joe Lookout and storage cabin.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: The cabin, at one point, was where the lookout actually lived. And then at the time all there was -- instead of the lookout tower, you were in a cupola. It was just a tall cupola, c-u-p-o-l-a. Anyway, it's a little skinny kind of a tower with a wee cabin where the lookout spent a certain number of hours looking out over the -- you know -- you had binoculars, and you had a map with an alidade -- that's another welding term. It's spelled, a-l-i-d-a-d-e -- almost like a crow's nest.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Right. But you didn't live up there?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Well, when I worked and when I became Little Joe lookout, the cabin was just a storage cabin; and I lived in the tower.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: How high was it?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: About 50 feet. Some of the lookouts are lower than others. It depends on the territory, what it needs to be looking out over. You know, if they need to be elevated so they can see across a certain range of mountains or see around a corner, so to speak, where a fire might start. This lookout, of course, had to watch over a thing called the cutout -- it had railroad tracks that went through. And that was sometimes a source of fires.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I see. And you did this throughout two fire seasons?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Uh-huh. Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay. And did that take you to the end of the war then, or what happened?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: That was when I went on my ride home, and that was the end as far as my shipyard work. And the war was officially declared over in July when I was up on lookout, and I had a shortwave radio. But I really, really, really, really wished I had been with my crew, you know. I could just imagine all the cranes' bells chiming and whistling and the shipyard and all the whoop-de-doo that they had in the shipyard. I really missed it. I missed all of that. I missed it.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That's kind of sad because you put so much into it.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I had really liked it and was doing something very important.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: It sounds like you were. I certainly do agree that you were. And that is your brother, Keith? {Looking at photograph.}

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: That was the one who served on No. 18 aircraft carrier, Keith Hamilton.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: These are wonderful photographs. You know, you didn't need any prompting.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: You know, I should have told you -- I was told by my older daughter living in California that she had gone to some kind of commemorative -- or a celebration at a shipyard -- at a Richmond, California, shipyard. And she met a woman there, a woman named Dorothy Bistodeau.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Can you spell that for us, please?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: B-i-s-t-o-d-e-a-u. And she's from Alexandria, Virginia, and my sister and she talked. And my daughter gave to Dorothy my address and asked, you know, because she was planning to write a book about women who worked in the war. So I had been in touch with this woman, and so I prepared a bunch of this stuff for her book that I thought she was going to do. And I heard from her a couple of times, but after -- I tend to think perhaps after 9-11, things changed for her. And maybe something happened, and I never heard from her again. She never, you know -- she was going to write a book called "Rosie the Riveter" or something like that. I had prepared a kind of a summary. It's in my file, and you're welcome to use it.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: It talked a lot specifically about the shipyard work and what, you know, how it progressed.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay. So why don't you talk just a couple of minutes, and I'll regroup with your file.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: It doesn't have to be in any special order at all. {Discussion and review of photos and Flora's material.}

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: You know, what is -- how did you eat -- how do I say this? When and how did you eat?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: You packed a lunch.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I was just wondering about everyday life. How did you eat? Where did you go to get food, and what did you eat? How did you store it?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: You know, some of that stuff is something I can't remember real well. It was not, you know -- I know that I managed to eat when I was staying with the Schwantes family, which is spelled S-c-h-w-a-n-t-e-s -- which was in Washington, with Sarah and Reuben.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And you lived with them for how long?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: year.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And when you lived there, I believe you said Reuben's brother lived across the street; and they were farmers --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Across the road; it was not a street. It was in the country.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And they both worked in the shipyard, and I carpooled with them.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: You carpooled?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: About 13 miles from Vancouver.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: 13 miles, okay.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: It worked out they could get gas because he was in defense work. They didn't have any problem with gas rationing.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I see. Were they working at the same --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I can remember Sarah when I guess it was -- something happened in Europe, because she was very, very German. Reuben was too. But Sarah was more -- tended more to emphasize it, to be proud of her German-ness. And she heard something on the radio and it really bothered her. And it came out then about how she felt about the war; she was not all that patriotic on either side. She minded it that the Germans had been bombed -- in a German place. I don't just remember exactly, but she supported Americans in the war too.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I can imagine there was a lot of that when the war was just about finished. And I think you should add -- do you have anything that you really don't want to forget?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: No, I was saying to my daughter I really would like some of that Rosie stuff to get in because I really thought it described the work that we did and, you know, some of the off-hours stuff that we did and the attitudes, you know, that Rosie had -- what Dorothy Bistodeau had asked us was did we --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I'm sorry. Who --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Bistodeau, I think her name was Dorothy Bistodeau.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Gotcha.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: -- asked about whether there was absenteeism, was there, you know, was there grumbling and that sort of thing. And actually, what I told her was absolutely not. You know, people showed up, and they did their jobs. There wasn't a lot of goofing off, you know, because a lot of those stories kind of go around in some areas about how people screw up and, you know --

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: You know what I think would be a good story, Mom, although it's kind of emotional, but that guy who saved those lives by blowing that whistle, you know, when he knew --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Oh. Yeah. That was a part of the Rosie thing. This was one night, you know, as I said, I worked swing shift, so it was after ten clock at night. And the "whirly" cranes -- they are these great tall cranes -- and they have four legs, and they had a boom on the top that, you know, can go 360 degrees. And when they were lifting a heavy section of ship that had been completed and we had worked on and was out in the subway between our building and the ways themselves -- and sometimes it would take two cranes to carry one of these sections.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: They were heavy.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Heavy sections. And you know this was late one night, and two of the cranes were out there moving a big section; and one of them started to go down. And it would have gotten, you know, shipfitters and people guiding the cranes, you know, from the ground too. And this one crane operator started blowing his whistle. And he just blew it and blew it because it was an alarm and managed to get everybody out -- out from under this big section that could have been killed by the section dropping.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: He died.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. He died.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: Because it was his crane and it fell down.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. It collapsed.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: What a sacrifice.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: He really cared.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: He tried to save as many as he could.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. We had a woman -- the overhead cranes that ran on, they ran on tracks. They had cables that held the sections, you know, and there was a track on each side of each big bay. These bays, as I said, were about -- I don't remember -- 75 feet wide and hardly, you know, way, way up.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Higher than you can count.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And it was break time, which must have been about 6:00 or something like that. I remember the times because it was swing shift. This -- it had been raining, and the crane, of course, would have been out in the -- could have been out in the rain because the tracks ran outside of the bay to pick up material from the -- from the -- what do they call them --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Supply thing?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Anyway, people that mark things up. And she came in, and she was to meet her husband down in the break room down on the level, you know, on the base. And she fell; and this was about a 60-foot -- probably a 60-foot fall.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Oh, my.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Maybe something like 45 feet, but she fell right on the metal. And of course, she died.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: She was a crane operator?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Uh-huh. One of the overhead cranes -- there's kind of a little cabin up there, but it goes along parallel.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: It hangs, kind of?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: No, it doesn't hang. It runs on rails --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: On the rails --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And it just runs parallel to the bay, to the way where we were doing the work.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: So you had some casualties where you were?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. I'm amazed that more people didn't hurt themselves because we had to learn to walk over those railroad track things, you know, over -- suspended above, you know, about 3 feet above concrete. And it would have been so easy to fall. And there was a lot of slippery stuff, like the flux from welders, you know, it's really like a slippery sand. And you know, we could have taken a real fall. But nobody did.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: How many were there in your group?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Our crew was -- how many were there? Eight, nine in my crew. {Interviewer and daughter reviewing photographs.} Just the women.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Eight. You were one of eight.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And then there were, you know, shipfitters, several crews of shipfitters. I mean, the bay was quite long; so my crew, the crew that I belonged to, could be scattered over, you know, quite a -- probably -- my recollection of distances is not that good, but could have been scattered over quite a space in that area. We could have all been huddled anyplace.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Can you estimate how many of you in total there were with everybody's crew? Just a --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I would say maybe there could be -- and it would vary from way to way, I'm sure -- or from bay to bay because different sections would be working on different parts of the ship, you know, but probably 25 or 30 in or on one bay.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay. On each bay?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And there were 12 bays.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Twelve bays.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: In the building.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I keep saying building, but it had no front and no back. It just had a roof.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Well, that made it a building.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And you were the youngest person on your crew.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I found out from your little questionnaire here. What else would you like to add from this time?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Despite the fact that I quit school, I did go back and finish high school.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Good for you.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: After a bike trip and, you know, some speculation.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: No, the bike trip came after because you went --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: No, I came off the bike trip; and I started school.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: Oh, I thought you did the horse trip before that.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: So how did this relate with -- you had the horse trip which was the getting home from the war --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: From the --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. The bike trip was to go see a friend from the shipyards, a guy that I had kind of got stuck on but, you know, got over it when I had time. You know, sometimes space makes quite a difference anyway.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: We have a picture, but that picture I didn't bring with me. But that's why I think you went to high school before because the picture is from August 6, I think, or August 7 of 1947. And it was a roving photographer took a picture of her for the "Rocky Mountain News." Her brother had dropped her off --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: In Denver.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: In Grand Island.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: In Grand Island.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: And she took the train from Grand Island to Denver. And then she rode her bike, and it's a one-speed bike with these saddle bags on the back and basket on the front.Sandra Lacey:: Wow.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: And she rode her bike from Denver to Brownsville -- I kept thinking Galveston -- but Brownsville, Texas.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Actually, I shipped it. I left the bike in Alice, Texas, because I couldn't make myself ride the rest of the way. It was so bloody hot.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: It gets a little hot in Texas.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: Did you pick the bike up then 'cause you brought it up --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I left it there. I had it shipped to Corpus Cristi; and then I had it shipped to Denver because that way I rode from Denver to Alice, Texas. And then I rode from Denver to Montana -- to Missoula. I didn't do both, you know, both sides -- the full trip.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That's quite an undertaking I would think. Anything else that you can think --Flora Fieldman:: I'm the "Undertaker."

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Not that kind of undertaking. Don't be saying that.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Anyway. Some of the stuff in here I think describes some of the actual work being done, you know, and the attitudes of the people. And I think that those are important, you know, the lack of absenteeism and the lack of goofing off.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And about the women -- I read something in here about how they weren't patronized?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: No. We weren't lead person. We had a lead man always, you know, but actually they weren't -- I don't think that we were put down because of being women at all.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And at that time, that's a huge issue.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: That's right, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That's wonderful.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And actually I'm sure that women, all in all, are better welders than men. I do think so. I think they pay more attention to detail. And, like, you want to make it look pretty; but you wanted it to do the job.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And what did you do in any spare time that you had?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Oh, listened to the radio and occasionally go on, you know, a date. And there would be functions that the shipyard would put on from time to time, you know, picnics or beauty contests -- they had a couple of those, a Miss something or other, you know. So there were things to do -- go to the seacoast.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Movies?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Dancing?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: You did those things? And roller skating?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: And what was that hula thing?

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Hula thing?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Oh, that was this gal that her boyfriend was in the Navy; and he sent her a grass skirt and outfit from Hawaii. And we'd get together at somebody's house, you know, we'd -- Kay Lanning was another, she was one of the crew.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: On your crew?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And how do you spell her name?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Lanning. It was K-a-y L-a-n-i-n-g. MS. LISA HAMILTON-FIELDMAN FIELDMAN: I think it was 2 n's. You have 2 n's in here, anyway.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yeah, I bet it was. Two n's. Anyway, she was always clowning; and she would model her welding outfit.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Oh. Oh, there she is. {Looking at photograph.} Kay Lanning.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: The "Funny Girl." And Mary Murphy.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And Mary Murphy was --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Is the one that -- she was a welder, and she had the boyfriend in the Navy and was in Hawaii and sent her that.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And that was -- her first name?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Mary.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Mary Murphy. Okay.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And I have a question for you here. Is there a specific song that brings back special memories?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Umm ...

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Maybe Dinah Shore?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yeah. I really liked Dinah Shore. But there were a couple of others -- and quite a few of them were nostalgic, you know, like "Parting with a Smile." I forget who did that one.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: How about Glenn Miller?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yeah. I really liked him. I loved him.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: "White Cliffs of Dover?"

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Is that another one?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And "Something to Remember You By."

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yeah. Right. I can remember the song titles, but I can't remember the performers so much.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I think you told us most of that, Flora. Funny stories? Two brothers from Texas?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. The Rogers brothers. They would always kid you, like, You're from Montana -- "Baa-baa-baa." You know, think sheep. Sheep are not a big part of Montana, but you know they were funny, they were funny; and they made things, you know, lighten up. And you needed that.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Everybody needed that.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay. You were talking about the two giant cranes, the two "whirlies."

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: We have that story.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And about going to see the ship launched that you worked on?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And what about when Pearl Harbor was bombed? What were your feelings when you heard the news?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Well, then, we were still in Roundup at the time, of course, and I remember that I was standing in the room just ironing clothes. And I just stopped, you know; it was just like a shock wave. It really was for everybody, you know, in some way or another; and my dad was very much a radical and, you know, lefty. And I think even he -- you know he wasn't there at the time because he was in Missoula by then. But I think if he'd objected, he would have fought my going out to the shipyards and working.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: You think he would have fought that?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I think he would have fought that if he had felt anti -- you know, antiwar. Sandra Lacey:: I see.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: Well, and Mick signing up too.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: Mick signing up, he probably would have objected to that too.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. I'm sure he would have.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And that's your son?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: No, my brother.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I'm sorry. Your brother, right.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: He's Keith in the pictures, but he went by "Mick."

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Oh, I see.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Hamilton. Keith Bradley Hamilton. He came up with -- everybody knew him by Mick, so everybody said, Is that your other brother? You know, I had two brothers but --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I think --

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: You still have two brothers.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: How about that? Everybody's still alive.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: family of longevity.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: We're all still alive.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: You recertified after the war?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I was -- I welded for another five years.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: You did?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: After my divorce, I went back and recertified and worked on -- worked on such things as the Denver Convention Center -- no big roles, but --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And the Denver County Jail and things like that.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And it was also during those five years the economy fluctuated, and you had hurdles to overcome?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Sexual discrimination?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Not so much that as -- I worked at one place where I was invited to work at another shop. And I asked them, you know, would I -- would I be paid the same? And they said no, I would not. It was a nonunion shop. So I would not have been able to increase my pay at all. So then I declined; and I was eventually, you know, I was soon thereafter, I was let go. And I fought it through the union because it was obviously -- I had declined a job to work in a lesser, you know, a nonunion shop and would not have increased my pay at all. So I declined.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And what did you do after that?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Well, soon after that, this whole shop that I was working in had a bunch of layoffs because work did slow down. So I -- was that when I worked for 7-Eleven?

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: I think you worked for 7-Eleven when you were going to Opportunity School to be recertified. And yes, she worked for 7-Eleven and she -- I think she left, but after closing, had a paper route.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Multi-tasking.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: I think going to Opportunity School to recertify and yes, you -- and she left. And she had a paper route and -- but then after welding, then we also had the wreck.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And after that, we got involved in a -- we got rear-ended on I-25 and I --

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: She got hurt pretty bad.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yeah. My neck. I got a pretty severe whiplash, and so the doctor said it probably wasn't a -- welding wouldn't be a good idea. I think, you know, if I'd been working on flat surfaces; but when you're welding and looking up over your head and stuff, you know, that's not so good.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: An unnatural position --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That would have been hard.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: So then I went to work for the State. I just got kind of a temporary job in the Sunshine Room, which is a place where they kept all their, you know, the work of the legislature, the print, the printouts of the bills and all that stuff from the legislature.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: The Sunshine Room?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right. And they --

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: I don't think they call it that anymore, but they did then.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: No. Then after the Sunshine Room was closed for the -- the legislative season was over, I did some proofreading for the House and Senate records.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: You did?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That would be interesting to our court reporter here.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: And eventually I got a job with the State. I took a test for the State; and I got a position with the State and worked there for the rest of my working life.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: The attorney general's office.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: The attorney generals's office?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: What a fascinating life you've had.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Oh. It's really a hodgepodge, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Oh, it's great.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: It's a mixed bag.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: But gee, some of these neat stories. I bet we could go on for hours. I know I could listen for more hours.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Well, I'm sure we've used up our time and then some.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: I'm sure Pat is just --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Got sore hands.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Got cramps.

sp.speaker: Pat Boslough
sp.p: No. Your story is wonderful. I hope I've got it all.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Let me check and see if there are any last questions or anything you want to add from us having forgotten -- looking at anything you'd really like included to be archived?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Rationing certainly affected the way I rode home from the coast.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That would be the case. Shall we go off the record now? Everything else here would probably be anticlimactic after all your neat stories.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: Can we get a copy?

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: I'm sure you could. I think that would be very good for you to have a copy. We'll make certain of that. Before we go off the record, we'll put it in there. That's it unless there was something else you would like to add.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: I think I made reference to the Pearl Harbor attack and how that affected me and the rationing and how it affected all of us.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Do you need to fill out your forms?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Oh, yes, I do.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Well, we'll give you a few minutes to do that because they're going to do the closing ceremony in a little bit -- probably not very long, although we were kind of running late. I think maybe we have a few minutes. Nobody came to drag us out. I have enjoyed this so much, Flora.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Well, thank you. I have too. It's been kind of a -- you know -- a coming together. (Coordinator entering the room indicating five more minutes until end of interview.)

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: We could close now by my just thanking you again for everything that you did and for sharing and what a wonderful memory you have. There's been very little that didn't come just like that --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: After a little bit of twisting.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Well, there are things that remind you of other things. We'll make sure that you get a copy of this.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: That would be very welcome.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: And thank you very much, Lisa. And I do appreciate your help too. You really helped the interview and kind of helped us get off and running in areas we might not have remembered to do if you weren't a part of it.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: I was really happy to do it. And all of my siblings will be happy too.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Good. I'm so happy you did it.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: I am too.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Yes. And I am grateful to have been a part of it too. I really am.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Well, you know, it's a part of something that's not like the guys that were in service, you know.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Oh, I don't think you should sell yourself short. I think it's --

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: No, and I don't. Because I know that it would have been hard to rustle up that kind of a crew of work people, and you know, there were plants all over the country. It wasn't just shipyards, it was ammunition plants and all kinds of --

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: All sorts of different things.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Lisa Hamilton-Fieldman
sp.p: You know when you see that poster, "We Can Do It", if you look at that poster and then you think of her, especially how she looks in that crew, it's amazing. Because I think she must have posed for it. It really does. It really looks like her.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Okay. I will think of her.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Because there were mugs and posters and magnets and everything with that picture on it.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Oh, that's special. I would have liked to have been able to introduce you to my dad.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: To your daddy?

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: Uh-huh. You were born in November, right?

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: He was born in November too.

sp.speaker: Flora Fieldman
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Sandra Lacey
sp.p: That is why when you told me your birthdate, I just -- that is when it all came back when you told me your birth date.
